title: Malachi: turn the hearts (Malachi 3:23–24)
hookLine: the last prophet: Elijah will turn parents' hearts to children, children's to parents

lines: THE LAST PROMISE IS CLOSE TO HOME.
cards: After all of it, the burning coal on Isaiah's lips, Jeremiah's broken jar, the valley of dry bones, Jonah in the sea, the books of the prophets end with a handful of short verses at the close of Malachi.
First, a look back. In the King James: "Remember ye the law of Moses my servant." Then a look ahead: Elijah the prophet will be sent, before the great and terrible day of the LORD.
Then the last promise in the prophets. Of everything a prophet could hold out, a rebuilt kingdom, defeated enemies, a world made new, Malachi chooses something much closer to home.

teach.b: Here it is, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Listen for the direction. It runs both ways.
The Torah had already told children to honor their parents.
This goes further: parents turn too, and they're named first. Elijah's job, at the edge of the great day, isn't to win a battle. It's to get two generations facing each other again.
Readers hear that in different ways.

teach.h: THE HEART OF THE FATHERS TO THE CHILDREN.
teach.b: Some hear parents and children who've stopped understanding each other, and a promise that the gap will close.
Some hear the generations of a people, the old who remember and the young who will carry it on, turned back toward the same Torah Malachi just told them to remember.
It's the same Elijah who stood on Mount Carmel and went up in a whirlwind, the Elijah Jews welcome with a cup at the Passover table and sing about as Shabbat ends. Now, the hard part.
The verse goes on: turn the hearts, or the land will be struck with destruction. That's the last word of the book.

teach.h: READ THE PROMISE AGAIN, END ON HOPE.
teach.b: So when Malachi is read aloud in synagogue, the custom is not to stop on that harsh line, but to go back and read the verse before it again, the promise of Elijah, so the prophets close on hope rather than ruin.
Even in the reading, someone turns back toward the listener.

how: Malachi's closing verses are read in synagogue as a prophetic reading, including on the Shabbat before Passover, and by custom the verse promising Elijah is read again so the reading ends on hope.

o: the last of the Twelve, promising Elijah will turn the hearts
the prophet who went up to heaven in a whirlwind of fire
a judge who led the tribes in the days before the first king

games.q: turn the hearts — tap the pairs.

s: Malachi's promise is only about children honoring parents
it runs both ways, and the parents are named first.
the book's last words are a promise of hope
the last words warn of destruction, so the custom is to read the verse about Elijah again.
the same Elijah went up in a whirlwind
the Elijah of Mount Carmel and the whirlwind is the one Malachi says will be sent.

games.q: you're reading Malachi aloud in synagogue. the book's very last line is a warning of destruction. how do you end?
o: stop on the warning, as written.
read the line before it again, about Elijah.
games.why: by custom, the reader goes back and repeats the promise of Elijah, so the prophets close on hope rather than ruin.

practice: Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, a grandparent, a child, an older neighbor, a young coworker, and notice whether your heart is turned toward them, or a little away.

Then find one question you've never asked them, what was hard at your age, what do you wish someone had told you, and hold it, and their face, for a while. If you pray, you can say Malachi's line with them in mind.
